research: The August 2020 Cochrane pub3 review included 15 adult randomized trials (56,675 participants), with interventions lasting at least two years. Combined cardiovascular events were reduced (risk ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.70–0.98; moderate-certainty evidence), while all-cause and cardiovascular mortality showed little or no difference. This relative estimate is not a 17-percentage-point reduction or a prediction for this product.
context: A newer review, published online in December 2025 and in a 2026 issue, included 17 trials (66,337 participants). Its authors translated pooled effects into absolute differences at different baseline risks: below their thresholds of importance at low risk and potentially important at high risk. The overall mortality confidence intervals included no effect. Low-to-moderate certainty does not establish a guaranteed survival benefit; replacement nutrients and background diet matter.
debate: A 2025 review of nine trials (13,532 participants) found no statistically significant reduction in mortality, myocardial infarction or coronary events. It used narrower trial and endpoint criteria than Cochrane. Its included trials had bias concerns and largely predated modern statin care. The reviews overlap in underlying trials and must not be counted as independent replications. A non-significant result is not proof of zero effect; the review’s stronger recommendation against restriction is its authors’ interpretation, not a product verdict.

research: Morton et al. reviewed 49 randomized trials (1,863 participants) of protein supplementation alongside at least six weeks of resistance training in healthy adults not in an energy deficit. Compared with the same training without extra protein, pooled additional gains were 0.30 kg fat-free mass (95% CI 0.09–0.52) and 2.49 kg in one-repetition-maximum strength (0.64–4.33). Fat-free mass is not identical to muscle mass, and training contributed substantially more than supplementation. These averages do not predict results from this food.
context: The often-quoted 1.62 g/kg/day estimate describes total daily protein, not a per-meal amount or supplement dose. Its estimated breakpoint interval was 1.03–2.20 g/kg/day; the segmental-versus-linear model comparison was not statistically significant (p=0.079). It is not a proven personal requirement, hard benefit ceiling, absorption limit or toxicity threshold. This app does not turn that estimate into an intake target.
high: A 2018 review of 28 trials (1,358 participants) in adults without kidney disease found no significant difference in change in glomerular filtration rate between higher- and lower-protein diets. Interventions ranged from four days to 104 weeks; the review rated evidence low to very low. This does not establish lifetime safety, safety at unlimited intake, or suitability for people with kidney disease, who were excluded. Protein grams on one label do not establish kidney harm or reassurance.
